design_detail: Critical narrative review (Current Psychiatry Reports, Substance Use and Related Disorders collection, article 12, 11 pages) weighing recent reports on cannabis and psychosis, mostly 2013 to 2015 studies of people with schizophrenia or first-episode psychosis, against two hypotheses (cannabis as a contributing cause; shared vulnerability), with Hill's nine viewpoints as the structure. Two tables: seven studies on specificity (Table 1) and 14 mechanistic studies on plausibility with the authors' caveats (Table 2). No search strategy or selection criteria; 70 references.
can_establish: The shared-vulnerability argument as two authors made it in 2016, criterion by criterion, with pointers to the specificity, family, transition, trial and time-trend studies on which it rests.
cannot_establish: That cannabis does not contribute to causing psychosis: there is no systematic search or appraisal, the general-population cohorts and meta-analyses on which the causal reading rests are not reviewed, and the authors themselves judge most criteria consistent with either hypothesis.

sample.recruitment: Not applicable (narrative review). Cited studies are mostly clinical or registry samples: people with schizophrenia or first-episode psychosis, people at clinical high risk, national registers (Sweden, Norway, Finland), treatment samples (therapeutic communities, outpatients) and family studies.
sample.inclusion_exclusion: Not stated. The authors reviewed recent research reports, with two primary kinds of data: studies of people with schizophrenia and studies of first-episode psychosis (pp. 2-3).
sample.selection_effects: Selection by the authors. Among the 70 references there is no meta-analysis of cannabis and psychosis and none of the cohort reports pooled by Moore et al. (2007); population studies appear only as a 35-year Swedish conscript follow-up and a US national survey, cited for the existence of the association and for the gradient with heavier use, and longitudinal precedence is cited to the Swedish co-relative registry study. Laboratory studies of psychotic symptoms after THC are not discussed. Selected references are marked as of importance or of major importance, with one-line endorsements.

exposure.measurement: As in the cited studies: lifetime or current use, cannabis use disorder diagnoses, frequency (for example more than 21 times a year in Hartz et al.), age at first use, recent use by drug testing, and registry diagnoses of substance-induced psychosis.
exposure.dose_frequency_duration_route: Not synthesized. The authors argue that a naturally occurring gradient of use carries a gradient of associated confounders and so cannot show a pharmacological dose-response (p. 4).
exposure.polysubstance: Central to the argument: the specificity section and Table 1 present associations of psychosis with tobacco, alcohol, stimulants and opioids, and of cannabis with other psychiatric disorders, as evidence against a specific effect of cannabis.

comparison.controls: Varies by cited study: healthy or general-population controls, people with other psychiatric disorders, relatives of people with and without psychosis, treatment-as-usual arms.
comparison.unmeasured_premorbid: The shared-vulnerability hypothesis is itself a claim about unmeasured premorbid liability (a diathesis raising the chances of psychosis, other disorders and problem behaviours). The review does not discuss studies that measured premorbid factors and adjusted for them in general-population cohorts.

outcomes.instruments: As in the cited studies: diagnoses of schizophrenia or first-episode psychosis, conversion to psychosis in clinical-high-risk samples, register diagnoses, hospital admissions for cannabis psychosis, and brain imaging, post-mortem and biomarker measures (Table 2).
outcomes.validity_norms: Table 2 lists caveats for each mechanistic study (antipsychotic medication, other drug use not controlled, small samples, unreliable cannabis histories, higher education in controls); no caveats are given for the family, transition, trial or time-trend studies.
outcomes.operationalization: Psychosis and schizophrenia are used largely interchangeably.

analysis.effect_sizes: As cited, without intervals except where stated. Relative risk of psychosis about 2:1 with cannabis use and as high as 6:1 with heavier use (refs 1 and 18). Disability from the contribution of regular use or dependence to schizophrenia about 0.35% of the disability associated with cannabis and about 0.04% of that associated with schizophrenia (GBD 2010, Degenhardt et al. 2013), in a model that assumed earlier onset only. Table 1: Sara et al., 13,624 people with schizophrenia, 29% cannabis, 26% alcohol and 14% stimulant use disorder; Hartz et al., 9131 people with severe psychotic illness versus 10,311 controls, odds ratios 5.11 daily smoking, 4.62 recreational drugs, 3.96 alcohol more than 4 drinks a day, 3.47 cannabis more than 21 times a year; Nesvag et al., Norwegian register (9002 schizophrenia, 15,000 bipolar, 87,540 depressive), 5-year comorbidity in schizophrenia 14.8% polysubstance, 7.6% stimulants, 6.7% cannabis, 4.3% opiates, 3.3% sedatives; Auther et al., 370 at clinical high risk, cannabis association with conversion lost after controlling for alcohol. Finnish register: 8-year cumulative risk of a schizophrenia diagnosis 46% after cannabis-induced, 30% after amphetamine-induced and 5% after alcohol-induced psychosis. Trials in people with psychosis and cannabis use disorder: Danish, 102 outpatients over 6 months, more emergency admissions with the added therapy; Irish, 88 outpatients over 1 year, no effect on cannabis use or symptoms. Table 2 examples: 3.7% reduction in D2/D3 binding in the limbic striatum after THC (Bossong et al.); 8% higher prefrontal cannabinoid-receptor binding post mortem in schizophrenia (Volk et al.).
analysis.selective_reporting: Narrative selection. Studies supporting shared vulnerability are highlighted (for example a family study called well designed and a trial called well controlled) without limitations, while caveats are listed only for the mechanistic studies of Table 2.

interpretation_gap.results_show: By the authors' own criterion-by-criterion reading, consistency, temporality and biological gradient are consistent with either hypothesis, and the association is strong enough to warrant study. The case for shared vulnerability rests on lack of specificity (Table 1), three family studies, two clinical-high-risk cohorts and a Finnish register study, two small treatment trials in people already diagnosed, UK time trends taken from a 2013 commentary, and the absence of a confirmed biological mechanism (Table 2).
interpretation_gap.claimed: The abstract says the evidence reviewed suggests cannabis does not in itself cause a psychotic disorder (p. 1); the conclusion states, as the authors' belief, that this is probably "because cannabis does not in itself cause such an increase" (p. 9), and that research focused only on the cannabis-psychosis association will be of little value. Gaps: (1) the general-population cohorts that adjusted for measured confounders are not reviewed, so the evidence for a causal contribution is not weighed; (2) the GBD figure of 0.04% is offered as showing a small contribution although, as the authors say, the model assumed cannabis does not raise incidence; (3) two trials in people already diagnosed, one of which did not reduce cannabis use, are taken to suggest that large reductions in use might not reduce incidence; (4) the UK reclassification argument rests on changes in admissions while the authors doubt that use itself changed; (5) the view that a biological pathway is unlikely is supported by the point that the shared-vulnerability hypothesis does not need one; (6) residual association within the co-relative study is attributed to non-inherited factors such as season of birth, which monozygotic co-twins share (editors' appraisal). Against this, the review states plainly that the association is real and consistent, and that most criteria do not discriminate between the hypotheses.

timeline.event: Hill's criteria for judging causation from association (ref. 14), the review's structure.

Jessor: a 4-year longitudinal study of 432 adolescents finding cannabis use clustered with early alcohol use, early sexual activity, poor school performance and general deviant behaviour (ref. 8), the basis of the shared-vulnerability argument.
McLaren et al., review of cohort studies on a causal link between cannabis and psychosis (ref. 16), cited as suggesting the alternative explanation.

Gage, Zammit and Hickman, commentary in F1000 Medicine Reports (ref. 2): cited for a UK rise in cannabis use of at least 10-fold since the 1970s without a rise in first admissions for schizophrenia, and for the argument that it is better to warn while uncertain. Degenhardt et al., GBD 2010 cannabis estimates (ref. 24). Two trials of psychosocial treatment for cannabis use disorder in psychosis (Hjorthoj et al., Danish; Madigan et al., Irish; refs 65, 66) and a Finnish register study of substance-induced psychoses converting to schizophrenia (Niemi-Pynttari et al., ref. 63).

Family and genetic studies read as strong evidence for shared vulnerability: the Swedish co-relative registry study (Giordano et al., cited as 2014 online; ref. 39), an Australian twin and polygenic study (Power et al., ref. 59) and a US family study (Proal et al., ref. 60). Clinical-high-risk cohorts (Buchy et al., Valmaggia et al.; refs 61, 62) and a time series of UK admissions for cannabis psychosis around reclassification (Hamilton et al., ref. 64).

Di Forti et al., south London first-episode psychosis and high-potency cannabis (ref. 18), cited only for a relative risk as high as 6:1 with heavier use; tobacco analogies from a meta-analysis (Gurillo et al., ref. 26) and a co-relative study of smoking (Kendler et al., ref. 27).

Gage, Hickman and Zammit, published the same year, treat incidence trends as very weak ecological evidence and read the same co-relative study as showing overestimation of the population association rather than its absence.

Gillespie and Kendler read the same co-relative study (monozygotic odds ratio about 3.5 to 3.9, above 1) and a Mendelian randomization estimate of an effect of liability to cannabis use as good evidence against an entirely non-causal association.

replication.where_it_stands: The most cited statement in this reading list of the view that the cannabis-psychosis association reflects shared vulnerability. Its strongest points (non-specificity, familial confounding, the time-trend argument) are also taken seriously on the other side, where they lead to a partly-causal reading rather than a non-causal one: Gage et al. (2016) and Gillespie and Kendler (2021). Gillespie and Kendler read the genetically informed evidence, including the co-relative study Ksir and Hart cite, as against an entirely non-causal association. Claims should cite the primary studies for each figure and this review for the argument.

funding.declared_conflicts: The authors declare that they have no competing interests (Compliance with Ethical Standards, p. 9).
funding.affiliations_note: Ksir: Department of Psychology and Neuroscience Program, University of Wyoming. Hart: Division on Substance Abuse, New York State Psychiatric Institute, and Departments of Psychology and Psychiatry, Columbia University; Brocher Foundation, Geneva. None of the cited studies is by the authors.

what_would_settle_it: Designs that separate the two hypotheses: co-relative and twin analyses with cannabis use measured before prodromal symptoms; Mendelian randomization with instruments for heavy use; prospective general-population cohorts that measure problem-behaviour liability (early tobacco and alcohol use, school performance, conduct problems) before cannabis use and test whether cannabis adds risk beyond it; and controlled studies of psychosis incidence where cannabis use or potency changed sharply.

domains.note: No databases, dates or criteria; recent reports chosen by the authors, mostly 2013 to 2015 clinical studies.
Table 2 gives caveats for each mechanistic study, but the family, transition, trial and time-trend studies that carry the conclusion are presented without limitations.

domains.domain: Reliance on the authors' own studies
domains.note: None of the cited studies is by the authors.

Beliefs and predictions are offered as conclusions: no biological pathway is likely because the shared-vulnerability model does not need one; vulnerable people would start cannabis earlier than others; cannabis-induced psychoses are acute toxic episodes after unusually high doses (uncited); trials in patients are extended to population incidence. Several figures are uncited (age 16 at first use from a 2013 US survey; 90% and 10:1 comparisons for tobacco and alcohol).

domains.domain: Balance of evidence for a causal contribution and for shared vulnerability
domains.note: Under-represented: evidence for a causal contribution. Adjusted general-population cohorts and their meta-analyses, laboratory THC studies, and the residual within-family association in the co-relative study are not weighed, while every non-discriminating criterion is counted towards shared vulnerability.

risk_of_bias.reasoning: No validated instrument applies to a narrative review (METHODS §5.3); the overall judgment follows the worst domains (search, separation of evidence from speculation, balance). The review is useful for setting out the shared-vulnerability argument and the non-specificity data clearly, and it is candid that most criteria do not discriminate; but its conclusion that cannabis probably does not itself raise psychosis risk is not supported by the evidence it presents, which is selected and appraised asymmetrically. It may be cited for the argument and as a pointer to the specificity, family, transition and trial studies; figures must be cited to their primary sources.

key_findings.finding: Points the authors accept: people with first-episode psychosis or schizophrenia are more likely to report current or prior cannabis use than the general population, an association reported so often that it cannot be dismissed (recent data from Italy, the USA, Sweden, France and South Africa); cannabis use clusters with other problem behaviours (Jessor 1976, a 4-year study of 432 adolescents); schizophrenia is linked with many other variables. Interest has grown from fewer than 10 papers a year in the 1990s to over 100 a year since 2012 (PubMed).

Method: a review of recent research reports for the evidence each gives on two hypotheses, cannabis as a contributing cause and shared vulnerability; two primary kinds of data, studies of people with schizophrenia and studies of first-episode psychosis; Hill's nine viewpoints as the structure. No search or selection method is described.

Shared-vulnerability hypothesis: a diathesis raises susceptibility to psychosis and to other disorders, including substance use disorder, and to problem behaviours, which emerge at different ages; with first use at a self-reported age of 16 in the 2013 US national survey and schizophrenia onset in the early 20s in men, cannabis use would precede diagnosis without causing it; early and heavy use are seen as possible prodromal signs.
key_findings.note: The age-16 figure has no citation.

key_findings.finding: Strength: relative risk about 2:1, and as high as 6:1 for heavier use, plus earlier onset of psychosis in people who use cannabis; weaker than tobacco and lung cancer or alcohol in pregnancy and birth defects (risk ratios given as about 10:1, uncited) but strong enough to warrant study. A Global Burden of Disease model (ref. 24) put the disability from the contribution of regular use or dependence to schizophrenia at about 0.35% of the disability associated with cannabis and about 0.04% of that associated with schizophrenia; the authors note that the model did not accept that cannabis raises incidence and counted earlier onset only. They conclude research should be motivated by understanding schizophrenia rather than by hopes of reducing its burden.

Consistency, temporality and gradient: consistency is solid but favours neither hypothesis; temporality favours a causal role only against self-medication, and with first use typically five or more years before a first psychotic episode it gives no special support; heavier use carries greater risk, but a naturally occurring gradient of use also carries associated confounders, so the dose-response findings are consistent with either hypothesis.
key_findings.locator: Literature Review › 2. Consistency (p. 3); 4. Temporality (pp. 3-4); 5. Biological Gradient (p. 4)

key_findings.finding: Specificity (Table 1): Sara et al., 13,624 people with schizophrenia, 29% cannabis, 26% alcohol and 14% stimulant use disorder; Auther et al., 370 people at clinical high risk followed 2 or more years, cannabis abuse or disorder associated with conversion but not after controlling for alcohol use; Hartz et al., 9131 people with severe psychotic illness versus 10,311 controls, odds ratios 5.11 for daily smoking, 4.62 for recreational drugs, 3.96 for more than 4 drinks a day and 3.47 for cannabis more than 21 times a year; Nesvag et al., Norwegian register, 5-year prevalence of comorbid substance use disorder in 9002 people with schizophrenia 14.8% polysubstance, 7.6% stimulants, 6.7% cannabis, 4.3% opiates, 3.3% sedatives. Cannabis use is also associated with depression, anxiety, bipolar disorder and antisocial personality disorder. The authors read the lack of specificity as favouring shared vulnerability.
key_findings.locator: Literature Review › 3. Specificity, 1st to 4th paragraphs (p. 3); Table 1 (p. 4)
key_findings.note: The review does not say whether the Hartz et al. odds ratios are adjusted, or for what; the percentages are comorbidity prevalences, not comparisons with people without psychosis.

key_findings.finding: Plausibility: 14 mechanistic studies (dopamine, endocannabinoid system, brain volume and morphology, functional measures) are tabulated with caveats such as antipsychotic treatment, uncontrolled other drug use and small samples, and judged to give no consistent results supporting a pharmacological mechanism; genetic studies (COMT, copy-number variants, gene-environment interaction) are judged inconsistent. The authors state they believe it likely that there is no biological pathway from cannabis use to psychosis, since the shared-vulnerability hypothesis does not require one.
key_findings.locator: Literature Review › 6. Plausibility, 1st paragraph (pp. 4 and 7) and 2nd paragraph (p. 7); Table 2 (pp. 5-7)

key_findings.finding: Family-based studies: in the Swedish national registry, a clear association between cannabis use and schizophrenia, the majority of which disappeared after controlling for familial relationships; in an Australian twin study, greater polygenic risk for schizophrenia went with greater cannabis use; in a US family study, morbid risk of schizophrenia was raised in families of people with psychosis whether or not they used cannabis. The authors call these strong evidence for shared vulnerability over a causal contribution, and attribute any residual non-familial link to non-inherited factors such as season of birth, infections or birth trauma.
key_findings.note: No numbers are given for any of the three studies. Editors' cross-check: the Swedish co-relative odds ratios are given by Gillespie and Kendler (2021).

key_findings.finding: Transition studies: North American adolescents at clinical high risk, followed 4 years, level of cannabis use not related to conversion to psychosis (nor tobacco or cocaine use); in England, lifetime use did not affect transition but use begun before 15 raised risk; in the Finnish register, the 8-year cumulative risk of a schizophrenia diagnosis was 46% after cannabis-induced psychosis, 30% after amphetamine-induced and 5% after alcohol-induced psychosis, which the authors explain by cannabis-induced psychosis occurring mainly in people already at risk; alcohol-induced psychosis was reported over 100 times more often than cannabis-induced, and stimulant-induced 6.6 times more often.
key_findings.note: The over-100-times and 6.6-times ratios are given without counts; the size of the register sample appears only in the title of ref. 63.

key_findings.finding: Experiment: a UK rise in cannabis use of at least 10-fold since the 1970s, cited to Gage et al. (2013), and, without a citation, data on first admissions for schizophrenia showing no rise over that time, perhaps a slight fall; UK hospital admissions for cannabis psychosis fell after the 2004 relaxation of cannabis regulation and rose after the return to stricter classification in 2009, although the authors doubt the changes had much impact on use. Two randomized trials in people with psychosis and cannabis dependence: Danish, 102 outpatients, treatment as usual with or without motivational interviewing and cognitive behavioural therapy, more emergency admissions in the experimental group over 6 months; Irish, 88 outpatients over 1 year, no effect on cannabis use or on positive or negative symptoms. The authors conclude that reducing cannabis use in people with psychosis achieves little and that even large reductions in use might not reduce the incidence of psychosis.
key_findings.locator: Literature Review › 8. Experiment, 1st paragraph (p. 8) and 2nd paragraph (pp. 8-9)
key_findings.note: The UK figures are second-hand: the rise in use is cited to a commentary and the first-admissions statement to no source; the trials enrolled people already diagnosed and cannot test effects on incidence.

key_findings.finding: Analogy: no toxic agent is listed among risk factors for schizophrenia in DSM-5; the closest analogies are tobacco and stimulants; non-drug behaviours associated with schizophrenia (poor early school performance, violence among young offenders, arrest for arson) are read as markers of shared vulnerability, not causes.

Conclusion: the authors believe that studies have not explained how cannabis would raise psychosis risk, or found a way to reduce risk by reducing use, probably because cannabis does not in itself raise that risk; early and heavy use are more likely in people vulnerable to other problem behaviours, and in some the same vulnerability raises the risk of psychosis or another mental disorder. Research focused only on the cannabis-psychosis association will be of little value. Warnings about cannabis should avoid overstatement, which young people already distrust.

reporting_issues.issue: Table 2 lists Bossong et al. 2006 and Monteleone et al. 2013, but the cited references are Bossong et al. 2015 (ref. 41) and Monteleone et al. 2014 (ref. 53).
reporting_issues.consequence: Year errors in the table; identify the studies from the reference list.

reporting_issues.issue: The Australian twin study (Power et al., ref. 59) is said to imply that both schizophrenia and psychosis can be associated with some of the same genetic risk factors; from the preceding sentence, cannabis use and schizophrenia appear to be meant.
reporting_issues.consequence: Wording error; the finding concerns genetic risk for schizophrenia and cannabis use.

reporting_issues.issue: Figures given without a citation: age 16 at first use from the 2013 US national survey (p. 2); over 90% of cigarette smokers without lung cancer, over 90% of women drinking two or more drinks a day in pregnancy with normal-appearing offspring, and risk ratios of about 10:1 (p. 3); and the statement that cannabis-induced psychoses are acute episodes from unusually high doses (p. 8).
reporting_issues.consequence: These figures cannot be traced to a source and should not be cited from this review.

reporting_issues.issue: The Swedish co-relative study is cited as Giordano et al., Psychological Medicine 2014 (online first). Editors' cross-check: Gage et al. (2016) and Gillespie and Kendler (2021) cite it as 2015, volume 45, pages 407 to 414.
reporting_issues.consequence: The same study appears under two years across the three reviews; it must not be counted twice.
